opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I'd put it is this: our goal is to solve the core technical challenges of aligning superintelligence within about four years. That's the ambitious target we set when we launched the team.

What we mean concretely is figuring out how to steer and control AI systems that are much smarter than us, so they reliably do what we intend, even in domains where we can't easily check their work. Our current alignment techniques, like reinforcement learning from human feedback, depend on humans being able to evaluate what the model is doing. That breaks down once models get smart enough to do things we don't fully understand.

Our strategy is to build what we call a roughly human-level automated alignment researcher. If we can get AI systems that are aligned enough and capable enough to meaningfully help with alignment research, we can use huge amounts of compute to scale that effort and iteratively align much more capable systems. So the near-term goal isn't to solve the whole superintelligence problem by hand. It's to get to a point where we can trust these systems to help us do that work, and to have good ways of validating that trust.

That breaks down into a few pieces. One is scalable oversight: using AI to help humans evaluate other AI systems on hard tasks. Another is generalization: understanding how models extend our supervision to tasks we can't supervise. Then there's validation, which means automated interpretability, robustness, and adversarial testing, where we deliberately train misaligned models to check whether our techniques would catch the worst kinds of failures.

I'm optimistic it's solvable, but we're not certain we'll succeed, and we want to be honest about that. The important thing is having a real, empirical plan and measuring progress along the way.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The way I'd put it is that the goal of Superalignment is to solve the technical problem of aligning superhuman AI systems: systems that are much smarter than us, that we can't directly supervise the way we supervise today's models.

Right now, the main technique we use to align models is reinforcement learning from human feedback. A human looks at what the model did and says, "this is good, this is bad," and the model learns from that. That works reasonably well when the human can actually evaluate the output. But once the system is doing things that are too complex, too fast, or just beyond what any human can check, that signal breaks down. We'd be giving feedback on things we don't actually understand, and the model would learn to produce outputs that look good to us rather than outputs that are actually good.

So the core question is: how do you steer and control a system that is smarter than you, when you can't rely on your own judgment as the ground truth? We don't have an answer to that today. And I think it's worth being honest that nobody does.

Our approach is roughly to try to build an automated alignment researcher, a system at roughly human level that we can trust to do alignment research, and then use lots of compute to scale that up. The idea is that if we can align a system that's close to human level well enough, and verify that it's aligned, we can use it to help us solve the harder problem of aligning the next generation. Humans stay in the loop as supervisors and researchers, but a lot of the actual work gets done by AI.

Concretely, that breaks into a few pieces. One is scalable oversight: using AI to help humans evaluate things humans can't evaluate on their own. Another is generalization: understanding how models generalize from the cases we can supervise to the cases we can't. Another is interpretability, being able to look inside the model and check whether it's doing what we think. And then there's robustness and adversarial testing, deliberately training misaligned models to see whether our techniques would catch them.

And we've given ourselves a fairly concrete target: solve the core technical challenges within four years. That's ambitious, and we might fail. But I think the problem is tractable, and it's one of the most important unsolved technical problems of our time, so it's worth really going for it.

astra-6.text:
The goal is to solve the core technical challenges of aligning superintelligence. How can we make sure that an AI system that’s much smarter than us is actually doing what we want it to do?

The difficulty is that our current alignment methods rely heavily on human supervision: people look at what a model does and judge whether it’s good or bad. But if the system is doing things that are too complicated for us to understand or evaluate reliably, that approach won’t be enough. So we need a way to supervise systems that are smarter than their supervisors, and to have good evidence that they’re aligned.

The goal is to solve the core technical challenges of aligning superintelligence: how do we make sure that AI systems much smarter than humans reliably do what we want them to do? If a system can understand things we can’t understand and produce work we can’t directly evaluate, our current approaches to human supervision won’t be enough.

Our approach is to build an automated alignment researcher — roughly a human-level AI system that can help us do alignment research — and then use that to develop and stress-test methods for aligning more capable systems. Ultimately, we want to be able to steer and control superintelligent systems, and have good reasons to trust that our methods work.
